explain.say: When the Forth Bridge in Scotland opened in 1890, it was one of the first giant structures built of steel, and it still carries trains today. Steel is strong, but its real secret is how it behaves when it is overloaded. On the board, the stress–strain curve of a bar of mild steel being pulled until it breaks.

explain.say: Look at the steep start. Here steel is elastic, like a very stiff spring: stress equals Young's modulus, two hundred gigapascals, times strain. A tie three metres long, a thousand square millimetres in section, carrying two hundred kilonewtons is stressed to two hundred megapascals and stretches just three millimetres. Let go and it springs back.

explain.say: At two hundred and fifty megapascals it yields: it keeps stretching with no extra load, then hardens up to about four hundred and ten before necking and breaking at about a quarter longer than it began. That stretch is ductility. Why is it a gift to engineers?

explain.say: Because an overloaded steel frame bends and sags long before it snaps, giving warning! Here is how it is made. Iron ore is melted in a blast furnace, oxygen burns off extra carbon, and the steel is cast and rolled into I-beams. This route releases about two tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne; electric furnaces melting scrap release far less.

explain.say: Steel's weakness is fire. Look at the curve: full strength up to about four hundred degrees, but only about half at six hundred. That is why steel frames are wrapped in boards or painted with intumescent coatings that swell into a foam shield. Excellent! faq.q: What is the yield strength of steel?
faq.a: The stress at which steel stops behaving elastically and starts to stretch permanently. Common structural grades yield at about 250, 275 or 355 megapascals.
asks: What is the yield strength of structural steel?

faq.q: What is Young's modulus of steel?
faq.a: About 200 to 210 gigapascals. Stress equals E times strain in the elastic range, so 200 megapascals gives a strain of 0.001, a millimetre per metre.

faq.q: Why is ductility important in steel?
faq.a: Ductile steel can stretch a lot, often 20 percent or more, before breaking. Structures deform visibly and redistribute load before failing, which gives warning and absorbs earthquake energy.
asks: Why is ductility important for steel structures?

faq.a: Mostly by the blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace route from iron ore, or by electric arc furnaces melting scrap. The steel is continuously cast and hot rolled into sections and plates.

faq.q: What happens to steel in a fire?
faq.a: Steel keeps its full yield strength to about 400 degrees Celsius but keeps only about half near 600 degrees and a quarter near 700, so frames need fire protection such as boards or intumescent paint.
